stories.headline: India opens forensic labs to identify Nepal flood victims through DNA profiling
stories.title: India opens forensic labs to identify Nepal flood victims through DNA profiling
stories.summary: India opens forensic labs to identify Nepal flood victims through DNA profiling
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: India has opened its forensic laboratories to collect DNA samples from relatives of people missing in Nepal's flash floods.
The step could speed up identification of mortal remains and support grieving families across the border.

India will make the services of central and state-level forensic laboratories available to help identify the mortal remains of people missing after the flash floods in Nepal, the Ministry of External Affairs said on Thursday.
The move is aimed at helping first-degree biological relatives living in India provide samples for DNA profiling.
The decision comes as Nepal continues rescue and recovery work after the August 26 floods.
According to Nepalese authorities, the death toll has risen to at least 1,259, more than 12,000 people have been rescued, and around 5,000 remain missing.

The MEA said first-degree biological relatives in India, including father, mother, son, daughter or sibling, may have their biological samples collected and DNA profiles prepared at Central Forensic Science Laboratories, State Forensic Science Laboratories, laboratories of the National Forensic Sciences University, and NABL-accredited laboratories with DNA profiling capability.
In a press statement on Tuesday, the Embassy of India in Kathmandu had outlined the available information on procedures for identifying the mortal remains of the flash flood victims.

Against this backdrop, and as an additional step to support the ongoing identification process, the Union Ministry of Home Affairs has decided to make available the services of CFSLs, SFSLs and NFSU laboratories in India for "DNA profiling of first-degree biological relatives of persons who remain missing following the flash flood in Nepal", the MEA said.

Once prepared, the DNA profiles, along with the preliminary information required by the Nepali authorities, may be sent by email to dnacodis@nepalpolice.gov.np for comparison with DNA profiles obtained from unidentified mortal remains, the statement said.
For facilitation and coordination by the Embassy of India in Kathmandu, a copy of the DNA profile may also be sent to eoikathmandufloodsupport@gmail.com, it added.
The flash floods were triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal-Tibet border and devastated towns and villages in northern and central Nepal.

stories.headline: Bihar on high alert as Ganga rises above danger mark, 8 districts face flood threat
stories.title: Bihar on high alert as Ganga rises above danger mark, 8 districts face flood threat
stories.summary: Bihar on high alert as Ganga rises above danger mark, 8 districts face flood threat
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Rising Ganga levels have put eight Bihar districts on high alert as the state steps up flood preparations.
Tejashwi Yadav has criticised the NDA government, alleging inadequate relief, awareness and rescue arrangements.

Bihar is on high alert as the water level of the Ganga continues to rise, with the administration placing eight districts, Bhojpur, Patna, Saran, Vaishali, Nalanda, Begusarai, Lakhisarai and Jehanabad, on high alert amid the possibility of flooding in several areas.
The administration has also directed officials to alert people living in low-lying areas about the rising water level.
Local elected representatives have been asked to help spread awareness, while media, social media and public announcement systems will be used to share flood-related information.
The rising Ganga water level in Patna is a major concern.
According to the Water Resources Department forecast, the Ganga may cross its Highest Flood Level (HFL) at Gandhi Ghat in Patna on Thursday night.
At Hathidah in Mokama, the HFL may be crossed around Friday afternoon.
At Gandhi Ghat, the Ganga water level was 49.40 metres on the morning of September 1.
It rose to 49.98 metres by the evening of September 2 and reached 50.18 metres on the morning of September 3.
By 12 noon on Thursday, the water level had increased further to 50.25 metres.
The water level at Gandhi Ghat has now reached around 1.65 metres above the danger mark.

stories.headline: 1995-batch IPS officer Rajesh Kumar appointed Special DG CRPF
stories.title: 1995-batch IPS officer Rajesh Kumar appointed Special DG CRPF
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 3: Senior 1995-batch IPS officer Rajesh Kumar, presently Additional Director General (ADG) in the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), has been appointed Special Director General (SDG), CRPF, marking another elevation in a career that has included several significant operational and leadership assignments in Jammu and Kashmir. The appointment was approved by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) on Thursday. Kumar has been appointed to the Level-16 post of Special Director General on an in-situ basis through temporary upgradation of the post he currently holds. His tenure will be for two years from the date of assumption of charge or until further orders, whichever is earlier. Kumar belongs to the 1995 batch of the erstwhile Jammu and Kashmir cadre, now part of the AGMUT cadre. The official J&K Police gradation list records his date of appointment to the IPS as September 3, 1995, and identifies him as being on deputation to the Government of India as ADGP in the CRPF. His elevation is particularly significant for Jammu and Kashmir, where he has held a number of sensitive assignments during different stages of his career, including IGP Jammu, DIG North Kashmir Range, IG Special Security Group (SSG) and IG CRPF (Operations), Kashmir. One of Kumar’s important J&K assignments was as DIG, North Kashmir Range, Baramulla. In March 2013, following his promotion, he was appointed IGP Jammu Zone, replacing Dilbag Singh. At the time, Kumar was described as having served in several important assignments in the J&K Police. Rajesh Kumar moved to the CRPF on central deputation in March 2018, when he was appointed Inspector General in the force. The appointment order on the IPS government’s website records his induction as IG, CRPF, on February 28, 2018, while the J&K Police civil list records his deputation to the Government of India from March 12, 2018. His central deputation nevertheless kept him closely connected with Jammu and Kashmir’s counter-insurgency grid. In June 2019, he was appointed IG CRPF (Operations), Kashmir, replacing Zulfqar Hassan. The assignment came months after the February 2019 Pulwama terror attack in which 40 CRPF personnel were killed, making the operational leadership of the force in Kashmir particularly sensitive. He subsequently served in senior CRPF assignments outside the operational theatre as well. In March 2023, he was posted as IG, Administration, CRPF Directorate, before being elevated to the ADG rank. As ADG, Kumar once again became closely associated with CRPF’s Jammu and Kashmir operations. In 2024, he was serving as ADG CRPF. By 2026, Kumar was heading the CRPF’s J&K Zone as ADG. He was present in Srinagar for major CRPF events and was described as ADG, J&K Zone, during the force’s 88th Raising Day celebrations. The J&K Zone encompasses a large operational deployment of CRPF personnel involved in counter-insurgency, law-and-order and other internal-security duties. His deputation to the CRPF was also extended beyond March 18, 2026, by the ACC on the recommendation of the Ministry of Home Affairs. The latest elevation to Special Director General, CRPF, thus places a senior officer with extensive first-hand experience of Jammu and Kashmir’s security environment in one of the force’s highest operational leadership positions.

stories.headline: Stipend row turns into NMC, Supreme Court flashpoint
stories.title: Stipend row turns into NMC, Supreme Court flashpoint
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 3: With MBBS and BDS interns across J&K refusing to report for duty since August 31 in protest of the delay in stipend-hike, hospitals here are grappling with a severe crunch of ‘working hands’. The sudden withdrawal has left senior faculty and resident doctors stretched thin. The core of the matter is the debate on ethical work-load and commensurate emoluments to interns in view of the Supreme Court guidelines. At GMC Srinagar, GMC Jammu, SKIMS Bemina, GMC Anantnag, GMC Baramulla and GMC Handwara and other institutions, interns typically form the first line of round-the-clock care. They form a significant proportion of the staff deputed in emergency rooms, managing wards, and staffing OPDs through the night. The withdrawal of services has significantly impacted emergency rooms, wards and outpatient departments, according to hospital officials. There is no single official headcount of interns currently undergoing the mandatory one-year Compulsory Rotating Medical Internship (CRMI) in J&K. It can be gauged from the 1100 MBBS seats that J&K had in the 2020-21 session. Since the batch now serving as interns, plus BDS graduates, the total would be running into several hundred to over a thousand young doctors. This is estimated to be the largest simultaneous intern walkouts. Interns say their stipend of roughly Rs 12,300, that has been broken down as Rs 400 a day, is inadequate to meet their basic needs and has remained unchanged for nearly seven years. Protesters have cited Odisha paying its interns Rs 44,319 a month, West Bengal paying Rs 43,099 and Assam Rs 35,000. In J&K a 2023-constituted committee had recommended raising the J&K stipend to around Rs 25,000. This was later cited in the 2026 Assembly session as Rs 26,300. However, apart from the recommendations and a ‘file being stuck’, no other communication regarding thei has been received from the government. J&K Health Minister Sakina Itoo recently called the demand “justified” and urged interns against striking. She expressed concern that the withdrawal of services could negatively impact patient care. The NMC, responding to a Union Health Ministry query on the stipend issue in February this year said its CRMI Regulations, 2021 already provide for payment of stipend to interns. The actual implementation and quantum are decided by respective states and UTs, the NMC said. This, it said, is based on their own financial capacity and budget provisions. Months later, in June 2026, it told the Supreme Court that non-payment persisted at only seven of 756 medical colleges nationwide. Hearing a batch of pleas, the apex court directed that year that Army College interns be paid Rs 25,000 a month from October 2023. In October 2025 the SC rebuked the Commission, observing that its conduct deserved to be deprecated since the stipend issue had been pending before the court for long. The matter remains under the court's active supervision. A nodal counsel has been appointed in June 2026 to compile a state-wise compliance chart. Under the CRMI Regulations, 2021, interns have a defined middle ground in hospital hierarchies, working under supervision throughout the internship. They are not permitted to practise independently. They may assist but cannot perform major procedures on their own. Thus J&K's interns could assist in OPDs, ward rounds, emergency-unit postings and night shifts. However, their shifts often stretches 24-36 hours. There also is compulsory rural postings, making their work demanding and exhaustive. While the government has reiterating that the revised stipend proposal is "under process", the log-jam raises questions about ethical workload and stipend as per the guidelines and trends across the country.

stories.headline: Nepal Disaster: A Himalayan warning for J&K’s hydropower expansion
stories.title: Nepal Disaster: A Himalayan warning for J&K’s hydropower expansion
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 3: The catastrophe that struck Nepal should not be viewed in Jammu and Kashmir merely as another tragedy in another country. It is a warning from the Himalayas to the Himalayas. The August 26 glacier collapse near Langtang Lirung sent a massive mass of ice, rock and debris into the valley, triggering a devastating flood through the Trishuli river system. The disaster caused extensive loss of life and severely damaged hydropower projects and other infrastructure, with rescue teams searching for workers believed to be trapped inside project tunnels. Nobody can responsibly claim that hydropower projects caused the Nepal disaster. They did not. But the catastrophe has highlighted another vulnerability: when powerhouses, tunnels, dams, roads, construction camps and large workforces are concentrated in narrow and fragile Himalayan valleys, their exposure to extreme natural events can be enormous. Experts in Himalayan geology, hydrology and disaster management say the changing climate is making conventional assumptions about mountain hazards increasingly unreliable. They point to glacier retreat, expansion of glacial lakes, changing precipitation patterns, unstable slopes and the growing possibility of compound events involving landslides, avalanches and extreme floods. They caution that the issue is not simply whether an individual dam or tunnel can withstand a known level of hazard, but whether the cumulative concentration of infrastructure in a fragile basin remains safe when several hazards occur simultaneously. And Nepal is not the first warning. In February 2021, an avalanche of rock and ice in Uttarakhand’s Chamoli district generated a devastating flash flood down the Rishiganga and Dhauliganga valleys. The 13.2-MW Rishiganga hydropower project was washed away and the under-construction 520-MW Tapovan-Vishnugad project was severely damaged. More than 200 people were reported dead or missing. Sikkim followed in October 2023. A Glacial Lake Outburst Flood from South Lhonak Lake sent an enormous surge down the Teesta. The 1200-MW Teesta-III hydropower dam at Chungthang was breached, while roads, bridges, settlements and other infrastructure downstream were devastated. Experts say these events can no longer be treated simply as isolated, once-in-a-century occurrences. They argue that the Himalayan risk profile needs to be reassessed in the context of a changing climate. Jammu and Kashmir belongs to this same Himalayan system. Against this background, the question is whether hydropower development can continue to be planned on assumptions that may no longer adequately reflect the region’s evolving hazards. J&K already has a formidable hydropower construction programme. Pakal Dul (1,000 MW), Ratle (850 MW), Kiru (624 MW) and Kwar (540 MW) together represent 3014 MW of additional capacity, involving massive investment and extensive construction in the Chenab basin. The argument is not that projects already at an advanced stage of construction should be abandoned. The question is what should happen before another major project is sanctioned, another long tunnel is bored or another fragile stretch of river is subjected to intensive construction. Experts argue that J&K should consider a temporary pause on fresh large hydropower commitments to allow an independent cumulative reassessment of Himalayan safety. Such an assessment, they say, should go beyond the conventional project-by-project approach. One dam may receive environmental clearance, another tunnel may undergo geological assessment and another project may prepare its own disaster-management plan. But nature does not recognise project boundaries. A river basin is an interconnected ecological and geological system. Experts therefore call for cumulative assessments examining what multiple dams, tunnels, access roads, blasting, slope cutting, muck disposal and transmission infrastructure together mean for a basin. Such an assessment should map glaciers and potentially dangerous glacial lakes upstream, reassess landslide and seismic vulnerability, examine extreme-flood assumptions and determine whether dam and tunnel designs remain adequate under changing climatic conditions. Experts also stress that construction-phase risks deserve greater attention. Tunnelling, blasting, road cutting and disposal of excavated material can alter slopes and drainage patterns, potentially increasing vulnerability in already fragile terrain. J&K has already recognised some of these dangers. Early flood-warning systems are being pursued around hydropower projects and work on a GIS-based multi-hazard risk atlas has been initiated. Experts welcome these measures but point out that an early-warning system answers only one question: when might danger be approaching? It does not answer the more fundamental question: how much additional intervention can a mountain basin safely absorb? A warning system may provide valuable time for evacuation. It cannot eliminate the underlying exposure of a vulnerable dam, tunnel, road or construction camp located in a hazard-prone area. There was a time when exploiting every technically available megawatt of hydropower appeared synonymous with progress. Experts say climate change requires that assumption to be reconsidered. Technical potential, they caution, cannot automatically be equated with environmentally and geologically safe potential. The Himalayas have limits. Nepal has reminded the region of those limits at an unbearable human cost. Chamoli and Sikkim had warned us earlier. Jammu and Kashmir should not wait for a similar catastrophe closer to home before asking questions that can still be asked today. A temporary pause on fresh large hydropower commitments, pending an independent and transparent cumulative safety reassessment, need not amount to opposition to development. It can instead be an argument for development informed by what the Himalayas themselves are telling us. Nor does slowing further hydropower expansion mean compromising J&K’s aspiration for energy security. There is another vast source of energy waiting to be exploited — one that requires neither damming another river nor tunnelling through another mountain. It lies on the roofs of homes, factories and public buildings. That is where this "power talk" will turn next.

Experts welcome these measures but point out that an early-warning system answers only one question: when might danger be approaching?
It does not answer the more fundamental question: how much additional intervention can a mountain basin safely absorb?
A warning system may provide valuable time for evacuation.
It cannot eliminate the underlying exposure of a vulnerable dam, tunnel, road or construction camp located in a hazard-prone area.
There was a time when exploiting every technically available megawatt of hydropower appeared synonymous with progress.
Experts say climate change requires that assumption to be reconsidered.
Technical potential, they caution, cannot automatically be equated with environmentally and geologically safe potential.
The Himalayas have limits.
Nepal has reminded the region of those limits at an unbearable human cost.
Chamoli and Sikkim had warned us earlier.
Jammu and Kashmir should not wait for a similar catastrophe closer to home before asking questions that can still be asked today.
A temporary pause on fresh large hydropower commitments, pending an independent and transparent cumulative safety reassessment, need not amount to opposition to development.
It can instead be an argument for development informed by what the Himalayas themselves are telling us.
Nor does slowing further hydropower expansion mean compromising J&K’s aspiration for energy security.
There is another vast source of energy waiting to be exploited — one that requires neither damming another river nor tunnelling through another mountain.
It lies on the roofs of homes, factories and public buildings.
That is where this "power talk" will turn next.

In February 2021, an avalanche of rock and ice in Uttarakhand’s Chamoli district generated a devastating flash flood down the Rishiganga and Dhauliganga valleys.
Sikkim followed in October 2023.
The 13.2-MW Rishiganga hydropower project was washed away and the under-construction 520-MW Tapovan-Vishnugad project was severely damaged.

stories.headline: Reflections on J&K Bank
stories.title: Reflections on J&K Bank
stories.summary: Jammu and Kashmir Bank is not merely a financial institution in J&K; it is an institution with which people have a deep economic and emotional connection. Any discussion about its lending priorities, recruitment policy, board composition or corporate headquarters, therefore, inevitably acquires a significance that goes beyond conventional banking concerns. It is against this backdrop that Apni Party president and former finance minister Mr. Altaf Bukhari, during a recent press conference in Srinagar, raised several serious questions concerning the lending pattern, recruitment policy and representative character of the Board of Directors of Jammu and Kashmir Bank. He also referred to the possibility of relocating the bank’s headquarters. The party has sought clarity from the J&K government on these issues, particularly because the government remains the bank’s largest shareholder, with around a 52 percent stake. The questions raised by Apni Party need to be viewed within the broader framework of its political programme and ideological position. Following the press conference, the party president wrote an article titled “J&K Bank is Our Bank, Let It Remain So,” published in this paper on September 2, 2026, seeking to take the debate forward. Apni Party describes its ideological approach as a “center-ground, pragmatic and regionalist ideology,” focused largely on socio-economic development and safeguarding the rights of the people. The party has consistently sought to respond to what it considers the rational aspirations of the people of J&K, including the protection of land ownership and government employment for residents of the region. Its intervention in the functioning of J&K Bank is, therefore, also consistent with its larger campaign for employment opportunities for local youth and their meaningful participation in the nation-building process. But there is a larger issue here that political parties cannot afford to ignore. Across J&K, there is growing pressure on political organizations to address questions of economic insecurity, unemployment and declining opportunities. Political parties are increasingly being judged not merely by their political positions but by their ability to respond to the everyday economic anxieties of the people. The recent youth and student protests have only intensified these pressures. The Managing Director and CEO of J&K Bank, Mr. Amitava Chatterjee, has responded promptly to several of the questions raised by Apni Party leaders. His clarifications are important, but they do not entirely remove the need for a broader response from the government. Since the J&K government is the bank’s largest shareholder, the Omar Abdullah government also needs to articulate its position clearly. Transparency on these matters is essential if a trust deficit between the bank and the people is to be avoided. Before examining the bank chief’s response, however, it is important to understand the difficult economic and political environment in which these questions are being raised. First, political parties and opinion leaders in J&K are under increasing public scrutiny over the prevailing economic situation. The People’s Democratic Party (PDP), for instance, has presented a grim assessment of the J&K economy. Its senior leader Nayeem Akhter has highlighted concerns over low levels of government spending. Businesses, he has argued, are under considerable stress, with many entrepreneurs facing bankruptcy. Government spending has reportedly been curtailed, while contractors have become reluctant to take up new works. Concerns have also been raised about delays in the release of General Provident Fund (GPF) amounts to government employees and gratuities to retired employees. The real estate sector remains under pressure, while construction activity has also suffered. Former finance minister and noted economist Haseeb Drabu has, on several occasions, drawn attention to the difficult economic circumstances facing J&K and their possible long-term consequences. He has argued that the economy has performed worse over the past six years, with slower income growth, higher inflation and higher unemployment, even though the business environment has improved in the absence of bandhs. More importantly, he has pointed to the low level of credit as an additional constraint on an economy already suffering from a shortage of capital. In a capital-scarce economy, inadequate access to credit can have serious implications for investment, entrepreneurship and future growth. This brings the discussion back to the role of J&K Bank. As one of the most important financial institutions in the region, its lending policies inevitably have consequences for businesses, entrepreneurs and employment. The question is not simply how much credit is being extended, but also where that credit is flowing, who is able to access it and whether the lending pattern is adequately supporting the productive sectors of the local economy. The second major challenge is demographic. Economists and demographers have repeatedly warned that India’s youth bulge is expected to begin losing its demographic advantage around 2030. The transition could be particularly difficult if educational attainment, employability and job creation do not keep pace with the aspirations of a young population. The psychology of today’s youth also deserves greater attention. Young people possess considerable capacity to challenge established political institutions, but they may not necessarily have the opportunities, tools or training required to rebuild institutions in a constructive manner. A generation confronted by corruption, unemployment and political uncertainty can easily become disillusioned with conventional politics. In extreme circumstances, such frustration can create an attraction towards radical political causes. This is why employment cannot be treated as merely an administrative issue. The reported collection of ₹48.88 crores in job application fees by the J&K government over two years has become an eye-catching public issue precisely because employment has acquired such emotional and political significance among young people. Political parties and governments cannot afford to sleep over these concerns. It is in this larger context that the response of the J&K Bank management assumes significance. Mr. Chatterjee has assured that the bank intends to fill around 1,400 posts and that a notification for these positions will be issued shortly. He has also stated that these positions will be open only to J&K domiciles. If implemented transparently and expeditiously, such recruitment can provide a measure of relief to a large number of educated young people who are desperately looking for employment opportunities. The bank chief has also acknowledged the deep emotional connection between J&K Bank and the people of the region. On the question of representation on the Board, he has indicated that he would like to see Kashmiri representation, while making it clear that such an appointment falls within the prerogative of the J&K government. He has also ruled out any relocation of the bank’s corporate headquarters. These clarifications are welcome. Yet, the larger question of public confidence remains. J&K Bank occupies a unique position in the economic life of the region, and its future cannot be viewed exclusively through the lens of corporate governance or banking efficiency. Its relationship with the people of J&K has a historical and emotional dimension that makes transparency and accountability particularly important. The Omar Abdullah government, with the Chief Minister also holding the finance portfolio, therefore needs to provide its own considered response to the concerns that have been raised. Silence or ambiguity can create unnecessary suspicion, whereas a clear explanation can strengthen public confidence. The debate over J&K Bank should consequently move beyond political arguments and counter-arguements. What J&K needs is a serious conversation about credit, employment, representation, accountability and the role of its principal financial institution in supporting economic recovery. J&K Bank belongs to its shareholders legally, but its significance to the people of Jammu and Kashmir is much larger than its shareholding structure. It is an institution in which generations of people have placed their savings, aspirations and economic hopes. Preserving that relationship of trust must, therefore, remain a shared responsibility of the bank, its management, its shareholders and the government. Prof Gull Wani is Kashmir based Political Scientist

stories.headline: JERC retains green power tariff at Rs 0.50/unit in J&K
stories.title: JERC retains green power tariff at Rs 0.50/unit in J&K
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sep 03: The Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission (JERC) has retained the green power tariff at Rs 0.50 per unit for consumers in Jammu and Kashmir, while directing the power distribution companies to step up efforts to improve revenue collection and reduce shortfalls. The decision was taken while considering the tariff petitions filed by the Jammu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (JPDCL) and Kashmir Power Distribution Corporation Limited (KPDCL). According to the documents accessed by Rising Kashmir, the utilities informed the Commission that they were undertaking several measures to minimise revenue shortfalls and improve collection efficiency. These include plans to implement prepaid smart meters across 100 per cent of the consumer base. According to the petitioners, the prepaid metering system would require consumers to pay for electricity upfront, thereby reducing the risk of unpaid bills. They said smart metering had already been initiated to reduce unmetered consumption and address distribution losses. The utilities also highlighted amnesty schemes for defaulters, allowing consumers to settle outstanding dues with reduced penalties. They said the measure would help bring down accumulated receivables. Other measures include strengthening the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum (CGRF), expanding online bill payment facilities and conducting public awareness programmes on smart meters, timely payment of bills and energy conservation. The JERC acknowledged the measures and directed the petitioners to continue their efforts. On green energy, the Commission noted that the Ministry of Power (MoP), Government of India (GoI), has notified the Electricity (Promoting Renewable Energy through Green Energy Open Access) Rules, 2022, which enable consumers to procure and consume renewable energy. The Commission observed that green tariff is a relatively new concept in J&K and renewable energy development remains at a nascent stage. It, therefore, decided to continue the green power tariff at Rs 0.50/kWh, payable by interested consumers over and above the applicable tariff. Both high-voltage and low-voltage consumers will be eligible to opt for green power. Consumers can choose green power for 25, 50, 75 or up to 100 per cent of their consumption. The request will have to be made for a minimum period of one year, while the distribution licensee will be required to process applications within 30 days. The JERC has also directed JPDCL and KPDCL to give wide publicity to the scheme and submit its outcome in their next tariff petition.
